sections.text: Lord Shri Krishna said: I will now reveal to thee, since thou doubtest not, that profound mysticism, which when followed by experience, shall liberate thee from sin.
This is the Premier Science, the Sovereign Secret, the Purest and Best; intuitional, righteous; and to him who practiseth it pleasant beyond measure.
They who have no faith in this teaching cannot find Me, but remain lost in the purlieus of this perishable world.

We have started discussing chapter nine, which is the Raja Vidya Rajaguhiya Yoga, the Yoga of the Royal Knowledge and Royal Secret. This is in continuation of what we have discussed in the last two chapters, 7 and 8. In chapter 7 we have seen Gnana Vignana Yoga, Yoga of Knowledge, and Visishtha Gnana, which is applied knowledge -- or what we call wisdom. Wisdom is something we have gained through our own experience. As the saying goes, Look at my gray hair. I didnt get this gray hair standing in the sun outside -- all this is experience. In other words, what I have learned through my experience became my own knowledge.
Somebody told me something that remained at the information level, then I applied it and it became my own knowledge. Thats why in science college you have theoretical classes and then you go to the lab. The same thing you learned there -- that H2O makes water -- you go and experiment with it yourself, and you realize thats what happens. So the first thing we did after finishing the first six chapters was talk about who we are and how we purify our internal instrument by meditation, by all these sadhanas, selfless actions. Now the question is: what are we meditating upon? That is what we need to know. So from chapter seven onward, we started talking about self-knowledge -- knowledge about my own self, removing this paradox where I think this is me and still worry about what happens to me after death and what happened before my birth.
So the self-knowledge, the Gnana Vignana Yoga, tells us what is the nature of the Lord and how people approach it. In chapter seven we learned about the Chaturvida Bhakta -- the four types of devotees. Everyone wants to achieve that state of perfect happiness where there is no sorrow, no imperfection in my life. In four ways we approach that. Our quest for that perfectness is described as Aartha, Jijnasu, Artharthi, and Gnani. One is approaching him out of distress.
One is approaching because he wants to gain something. One is approaching out of curiosity -- is there a state of perfectness? And the last one approaches because out of his own intuition, he knows there is a state of perfectness. Then in the last chapter we discussed the imperishable Brahman. Yes, there is a state which is infinite, imperishable. At that state of existence, we call it Brahman -- that which pervades everywhere and everything.
My world right now is pervaded by my thoughts, you know, and my thoughts are right now limited. So my world is limited. I can think about the things only which I have experienced in the past, you know, or I heard about it from others or something which I have known from reading the books. But my thoughts are limited to that. Therefore my world is also limited to that. Beyond this world, Im always afraid or curious.
What is beyond my thoughts? Before my birth, I can think about my life as far back as my childhood. I can think about my life in the future as far as I can think. So I had this guy trying to sell me an annuity, and he said this thing gives you lifetime income from whenever you start. I said, when can I start?
He said, you can start at age 70. I said, my lifetime may not be more than five or six years after that, so your lifetime income doesnt do much for me. He said, why do you say that? I said, by statistical data -- how many people in my family have lived beyond that?
So I know my future by observing what has happened in my family. So what is beyond that? Thats where I get lost. So Bhagavan said that imperishable Brahman is the state of yourself. So in chapter eight we have discussed about the nature of that imperishable Brahman and how I as this limited being fit into that.
That as long as I identify with this limited intellect in mind, this instrument of ego, I constantly come back and forth because Im hanging on to that identity. This me is where I am as long as I have that ego. Bhagavan says in the part of your Prakriti, hell come back again and again taking another instrument of transaction with this world continuing in the same argument. Now chapter nine says, now well talk about the royal secret. Why is it a royal secret? Because it is already obvious to you, but you are not aware of it.
Its right there, but I cant see it. Therefore its a secret. And its a royal science, because Royal -- Rajan, Raja -- connotes supremacy. In a kingdom there is nothing higher than a king. In our case we have the president as the highest authority.
But he has many people to question him and tell him what he is not doing right. In those kingdoms, the Raja was never questioned. Even though he is not wearing clothes, nobody says the king is not wearing clothes. There was a supreme status. They say this Vidya is a Raja Vidya, the supreme knowledge.
Beyond that there is nothing to be known. That is self-knowledge. I know physics, I know chemistry, I know all these things, I know all the knowledge about arts and everything else. But Bhagavan says there is only one thing you need to know -- about yourself.
And there is nothing more to be known. Therefore it is the supreme knowledge in the self knowledge. So the first verse of this chapter starts with Bhagavans profound statement: Idam tu te guhyatamam pravakshyami anasuya ve. I am going to tell you this. Gnanam Vignana sahitam yad Gnatva mokshyase asubhat.
Im going to tell you this knowledge along with Visishtagnam -- along with its wisdom, its application. Knowing that, you will be freed from what? From Ashubha and Shubha. Shubha is auspicious, that which is good. Ashubha is not good for me.
Anything in your life which you consider not good, youll be liberated from that. And we say, well, thats exactly what I was looking for all my life. Get rid of all the problems I have, Bhagavan, then Ill be doing your bhakti forever. Because right now I dont have time -- Im just fixing my problems.
My total attention will be yours after that. Bhagavan says, idam tu te guhyatamam. This knowledge which is the deepest, most profound secret. Guhyatamam -- guhya means secret, tamam means most. Im going to tell you. You know what is the supreme secret?
Its something nobody can figure out. Thats a supreme secret. Other secrets you can figure out by asking someone, but this secret is right in front of you, yet you cant figure it out. Like a person in disguise walking around in a party you see in a movie.
Everybody sees him but nobody figures out who he is. And he said, Im going to tell you this because youre anasuya ve. We have heard last time, youre a person who does not cavil or carp, who does not raise petty arguments or petty objections. Sometimes people come to a lecture to find out how smart the speaker is, to see whether he knows anything. Then they will find fault in it.
See, if you give an example and say, our life is short, but the sun is there forever, suddenly somebody says, well thats not true, the sun is not there forever. I can tell you how it works. But that was not the intention of the speaker in giving that analogy -- to give you a relationship. But because your purpose is only to see what the speaker does not know.
So you are carping at him, raising petty objections, pointing out petty faults and errors. Because you are not truly, genuinely interested in understanding. The person who is like that is obviously not going to learn, because his mind is not in learning things -- his mind is in finding out where the faults lie. So therefore he says, Im going to tell you the deepest of secrets, the most profound secret. Because so far you have proved that you are a genuine seeker of this knowledge. You really want to find out how to get rid of sorrows from your life, how to readjust your thinking pattern so you can function right in this world. Having known the Gnanam vignana sahitam yad gnatva mokshyase asubhat -- after that you will get rid of all that is ashubha, sorrowful, not conducive in your life.
Bhagavan, thats what Ive been looking for! If you can tell me, then after this, once I know: every time I buy a lottery, Ill be the winner. Every time I submit a proposal, Ill be the winner. Every time I put a contract on a property, Ill be the winner -- because you told me that after knowing this, there will not be any sorrow in your life.
Youll be just a winner. Youll never be a loser. Bhagavan said, thats not what it means. What it means is that after knowing this, you will not see anything happening in your life as inherently good or bad. Right now, my definition of good and bad is defined by what I want and what I want to reject. Everything which I want to reject is Ashubha. Everything I want is Shubha.
There is a story of a father who goes to visit his two daughters. One was married to a pot maker, another was married to a farmer. He went to the daughter married to the farmer and said, Whats happening? She said, Oh, this was a wonderful season, a lot of rains, and we are doing very well. Oh Lord, keep continuing doing that! Then he goes to the other daughters house, the one married to the pot maker. So how are things going? She said, Pretty bad this year. There was no sun. It was raining all the time. We couldnt really bake any pots, so we are really not doing well. Hope the Lord does something and stops this rain. So the father thinks, Oh Lord, please stop this rain so that my daughter will be happy. But what can a father do? Same situation -- one sees it as Shubha, the other sees it as Ashubha.
The Shubha and Ashubha, as we are saying, are projections of our mind. We create this Shubha and Ashubha in our life. Once I fix my perception of how to see the world, I may not find anything Ashubha in it.
Theres this story in the Mahabharata. Yudhishthir and Duryodhan were both under the same teacher. The teacher said, I have one test for both of you. He calls Yudhishthir first and says, Go and find one bad person from this town. Yudhishthir goes off. Then he called Duryodhan and said, Go and find one good person from this town. After a while, Yudhishthir comes back. The teacher asks, Where is the bad person I asked you to bring? He said, Im so sorry, but I couldnt find anybody bad in this town. Then Duryodhan comes back. Where is the good person I asked you to bring? He said, Im so sorry, but I couldnt find any good person in this town. Both have a different way of looking at the world.
One cannot find anything bad in this world other cannot find anything good in this world. I right now have divided my world into good and bad because of my attachment, my desires, my aspirations of what I want to achieve. When I achieve that, great. When I dont achieve that, the world is falling apart. Bhagavan said, having known this knowledge, there will not be Ashubha in your life.

Krishna promises to reveal the most profound mysticism (guhyatamam) - knowledge combined with direct experience (jnana with vijnana) that liberates us from all that is inauspicious (ashubha). But this royal secret is only accessible to those who approach without caviling or carping (anasuya) - without petty objections or the desire to find fault. Today, examine your relationship with spiritual teachings: Do you approach them as a genuine seeker, or do you sometimes listen just to critique? The mind that seeks faults in the teaching never receives its nectar.
The chapter opens with a powerful reframe: what we label as good and bad (shubha and ashubha) are merely projections of our desires. Like the story of Yudhishthira who could find no bad person, and Duryodhana who could find no good person - each saw the world through the lens of their own nature. This week, when something bad happens, pause and ask: Is this truly ashubha, or have I simply labeled it so because it conflicts with what I want? Krishna says that knowing this knowledge removes all ashubha - not because circumstances change, but because our perception transforms.
Practice exercise: Each morning, set an intention to receive the days teachings - from people, situations, and challenges - without immediately judging them as favorable or unfavorable. Notice how much mental energy is freed when you stop sorting experiences into good for me and bad for me.
